sentences.text: Every circuit in existence is governed by the relationship between three quantities: Voltage, Current, and Resistance.
Voltage (V) is the push, measured in Volts.
Current (I) is the flow rate of charge, measured in Amperes or Amps.
Resistance (R) is the opposition to that flow, measured in Ohms (Ω).
In 1827, German physicist Georg Ohm proved that current is directly proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance.
The Hydraulic Analogy: Think of a garden hose.
Voltage is the water pressure from the faucet, Current is the volume flow rate ( i equals d q over d t ), and Resistance is squeezing the nozzle ( R = V/I ).
Whenever electric current flows through a resistance, electrical energy is converted into heat.
This power dissipation is measured in Watts (W).
Standard through-hole resistors are typically rated for 1/4 Watt (0.25W) or 1/2 Watt (0.5W).
If you push 10 Volts across a 100 Ohm resistor, the power dissipated is P = V squared / R = 100 / 100 = 1 Watt.
A standard quarter-watt resistor in that circuit will quickly overheat, smoke, and burn out.
Golden Rule of Hardware Design: Always de-rate resistors by at least 50%.
If P = V squared over R = frac (10 V ) squared 100 Ohms = 1.0 W , a standard 0.25 W resistor will burn out.
Always select a resistor with power rating is greater than or equal to 2 times P dissipated
